title: Hall-Effect Bench Tour
description: Guided walkthrough of the strip current I, the applied field B, the transverse Hall voltage V_H, and what carrier density does to the signal.

steps.title: A strip, a current, and a field
steps.body: A flat conductor carries current along its length while a magnetic field points through its face. Nothing else is needed for the Hall effect — the whole demo is those two inputs and the voltage that appears across the strip.

steps.title: Step 1 — the strip current I
steps.body: The leads at each end of the strip push current I along it. Raise the drive slider and the carriers speed up; the lead glow and the particle drift both track I. On its own this current produces no transverse voltage at all.

steps.title: Step 2 — the field B, local or coupled
steps.body: By default B rises with the same drive control — an isolated bench, honest about being self-contained. Turn on Lab field coupling and B instead follows the Halbach array's peak |B| estimate, clamped to this bench's range. Either way it is a simulated number, not a metrology reading: watch the 'B source' line under the carrier buttons to see which one is driving the plant.

steps.title: Step 3 — V_H = I·B / (n·e·t)
steps.body: With both I and B present the Lorentz force pushes carriers toward one edge until the transverse E-field it builds balances it. The probe pair reads the result. V_H follows the product I·B, so halving either input halves the voltage — neither factor alone tells you what the meter will say.

steps.title: Step 4 — why probes are semiconductors
steps.body: Switch the sample from Semiconductor to Metal at the same I and B. R_H = 1/(n·e), and a metal's carrier density is ~1e28 m⁻³ against a doped semiconductor's ~1e21 — so the same field produces a signal roughly ten million times smaller. That ratio is the entire reason real Hall probes are semiconductors.

steps.title: What this model is not
steps.body: One algebraic equation over a lumped strip: no band structure, no temperature drift, no contact misalignment, no offset voltage, and no calibration. Coupled or local, the B here is a simulated estimate — this bench reports classroom numbers, never metrology.
